title: Reviewing two tests of AI ability

questions.question: Are the benchmark version, set of test problems and method for calculating scores identified?
questions.help: The benchmark version is the particular edition of the test, like an exam revised in a new year. This item concerns whether the edition, the problems used and the rules for awarding points are identified.

example.why: The test and scoring code are identified, but the paper’s results are not linked to an exact saved edition of the code and data.

questions.question: Are the ability being tested, the intended AI systems and the intended uses described?
questions.help: An ability is a skill the AI is meant to demonstrate, such as finding a rule in a pattern or answering a science question. This item concerns whether that skill, the types of AI being tested and the proposed uses of the results are described.

example.why: The paper describes testing AI on finding, understanding and applying engineering rules, to help researchers compare strengths and weaknesses.

questions.question: Are the test problems, the information provided and the required answers or actions described?
questions.help: A test problem is one question or puzzle given to the AI. This item concerns whether the starting information and the answer or action expected from the AI are described.

example.why: The paper describes the questions, supplied rules and drawings, and the answers the AI must give.

questions.question: Are the instructions, resources and limits for taking the test described?
questions.help: Testing conditions include the instructions, allowed tools, time, number of attempts and AI settings. These can affect the difficulty of the test.

example.why: Instructions and settings are described, but the exact inputs and software needed to repeat every reported run are not fully recorded.

questions.question: Is it described how answers or actions become scores and how results are presented?
questions.help: Scoring means turning the AI’s responses into a result, such as percentage correct. This item concerns whether the marking rules and the way results are shown are described.

example.why: The paper and code explain how responses earn points and how group and overall scores are reported. This does not mean every scoring choice is sound.

questions.question: Is it explained why the test problems measure the ability the benchmark claims to test?
questions.help: The test needs an explanation linking its problems to the skill it claims to measure. For example, remembering a fact and working out a new rule are different skills.

example.why: The paper explains why finding rules, understanding drawings and applying rules are relevant to working with engineering documents.

questions.question: Are the origins and choice of test problems justified for the benchmark’s intended use?
questions.help: This item concerns the reasons for choosing these problems: where they came from, how many there are, their topics and their difficulty, in relation to the test’s purpose.

example.why: The problems use real vehicle-design materials, but mainly one competition rulebook, with very different numbers of questions in each group.

questions.question: Were the test problems and the answers used to mark them checked for errors during development?
questions.help: Reference answers are the supplied answers used to mark the AI’s work. This item concerns checks for mistakes in both the problems and those answers while the test was being made.

example.why: Additional reviewers checked many questions, but some questions and explanations received less checking than others.

questions.question: Is there evidence that the test problems cover the relevant parts of the ability being claimed?
questions.help: A claimed skill may have several parts. A test of science knowledge, for example, may need questions from several branches of science rather than just one.

example.why: The test covers several useful engineering-document skills, but one rulebook and six question types cannot establish coverage of all engineering work.

questions.question: Is there evidence that the way points are awarded reflects the ability the benchmark is meant to measure?
questions.help: This item concerns whether earning more points reflects doing better at the intended skill. A score can also be affected by details such as the required answer format.

example.why: Correct yes/no answers earn credit, but missing commas or different wording can also reduce scores even when an answer is useful.

questions.question: Is there evidence supporting how scores are combined and what any separate scores are said to measure?
questions.help: An overall score combines results from different problems. Separate scores may describe particular subjects or skills. This item concerns support for those choices and interpretations.

example.why: The question groups have clear purposes, but giving all six groups equal weight has not been shown to produce a meaningful overall ability score.

questions.question: Was the marking process tested to see whether it awards the right scores consistently?
questions.help: Marking may be done by people, fixed software rules or another AI. This item concerns whether the marking was tested for correct and consistent decisions.

example.why: Small marking-test files and reported scoring problems show some checking. A full study of whether the marks are correct and consistent was not established.

questions.question: Are the comparison points used to explain the scores justified for the claims being made?
questions.help: A comparison point is a result used to help interpret an AI’s score, such as a human score, another AI’s score or the score expected from guessing. The comparison needs to fit the claim being made.

example.why: Other AI systems and random guessing provide comparisons, but there is no reported human-engineer baseline, and some systems receive different information.

questions.question: Was it tested how much the same AI system’s score changes when the benchmark is run more than once?
questions.help: A repeated run means testing the same AI again under the same conditions. This item concerns whether researchers measured how much its score changes across those runs.

example.why: One AI was tested with five different sets of rule passages. This gives limited repeat information, but does not isolate score changes under identical conditions.

questions.question: Was it tested how much scores change when instructions, presentation or the testing setup change?
questions.help: The same problems can be presented with different wording, layouts or software settings. This item concerns whether the effect of those changes on scores was measured.

example.why: The paper tests changes to supplied passages and images, but does not examine every important change to instructions or settings.

questions.question: Are estimates of how much scores could vary provided in enough detail to support the comparisons or decisions being made?
questions.help: A range around a score describes uncertainty under the method used to calculate it. This item concerns whether that information is detailed enough for the conclusions drawn from the scores.

example.why: The main comparisons lack enough information about score variation to judge small differences confidently. A limited side experiment does report some variation.

questions.question: Were ways of earning points without using the ability being tested investigated?
questions.help: An AI might gain points from accidental clues or guessing rather than the intended skill. This item concerns whether such possibilities were investigated.

example.why: The paper examines some unwanted influences on scores, such as wording and formatting, but does not fully test ways to gain points without engineering understanding.

questions.question: Was the risk that AI systems had already seen the test problems or answers assessed and addressed?
questions.help: An AI may remember a problem or answer encountered during training. This item concerns whether that risk was examined and steps were taken to reduce it.

example.why: The authors discuss new images and possible prior exposure, but do not directly check what every AI saw during training.

questions.question: Are the rules on training specifically for this test and repeatedly submitting results justified for the intended use?
questions.help: Training specifically for a test means changing an AI to improve its results on that test. Repeated submissions can provide feedback for further changes. This item concerns whether the rules for both fit the test’s purpose.

example.why: The reviewed sources do not provide clear enough rules on training on the questions and repeated submissions to judge whether those rules are suitable.

questions.question: Is there evidence for any claim that the scores show how well an AI system will perform beyond the problems in this test?
questions.help: A claim about performance beyond the test predicts success on other problems or real work. This item concerns evidence for such predictions, when they are made.

example.why: Realistic vehicle problems do not show that scores predict success on other rulebooks or real engineering projects. No such study was established in the reviewed sources.

questions.question: Is there evidence that comparisons are fair across the AI systems and situations the benchmark is meant to cover?
questions.help: AI systems may receive different information, tools or problem sets. This item concerns whether comparisons remain fair and meaningful across the systems and situations the test is meant to include.

example.why: Settings are described, but some systems receive the whole rulebook and others only selected passages. Those results compare the AI together with its information supply.

questions.question: Are the test materials and methods available in enough detail for someone else to repeat the evaluation or examine how it was done?
questions.help: Test materials include problems, marking rules, instructions and software. This item concerns whether enough is available to repeat the evaluation or inspect how it was carried out.

example.why: Questions, scoring code and some AI outputs are public, but the materials do not form a complete record for reproducing every published result.

questions.question: Are the rules for accessing and reusing the benchmark, and the protections needed for responsible use, stated?
questions.help: Access and reuse rules explain who can obtain, share or modify the materials. Protections may include keeping hidden answers private or limiting harmful content.

example.why: Access instructions are available, but complete reuse permissions and responsible-use rules were not found in the reviewed sources.

questions.question: Are changes to the benchmark recorded, including how they affect comparisons between old and new scores?
questions.help: A test can change when problems, answers or marking rules are revised. This item concerns whether those changes and their effects on comparisons with earlier scores are documented.

example.why: Code history identifies revisions, but a clear record explaining how changes affect old and new scores was not found.

questions.question: Do the published claims stay within what the evidence supports?
questions.help: Published claims are statements about what a score shows the AI can do. This item concerns whether those statements fit what the available findings establish.

example.why: The paper explains important limits, but broad statements about engineering understanding and precise rankings still need more support.

benchmarks.name: ARC-AGI-2
benchmarks.subtitle: Learning rules from coloured grids
benchmarks.scope: ARC-AGI-2 public test problems, the official scoring software, and ARC Prize’s rules for tests that it runs or verifies. Sources were inspected on 7 October 2026. Other competitions and community results may use different rules.
benchmarks.overview: Each puzzle shows several before-and-after grids of coloured squares. The AI must infer the hidden rule and produce outputs for new inputs. Public development tasks are available for practice; separate tasks are used for evaluation. You do not need to solve the puzzles to complete this survey.
benchmarks.intended_use: Using scores to compare AI systems’ ability to solve unfamiliar grid problems, and considering the creators’ broader claims about reasoning.

facts.text: The release lists 1,000 public development tasks and three evaluation sets of 120 tasks each. Exact public-data and scorer versions are identified for this packet; hidden tasks are not supplied.
The stated goal is abstract problem-solving on unfamiliar tasks, requiring little specialist knowledge. The creators connect this to progress toward more general, human-like AI.
Each task gives input/output grid examples and new input grids. The system must supply the missing outputs, including their size and cell colours.
Two attempts are allowed per input. Verified testing specifies model settings and a cost cap; other evaluation routes can differ.

The inspected scorer checks grid equality, averages successes across test inputs within a task, then across tasks. A task with one of two inputs solved receives 0.5. The dataset description calls a task solved only when all inputs are correct.

The creators aim to test learning a new transformation from examples, rather than recalling facts. Their design goals include combining concepts and reducing success through exhaustive trial-and-error search.
Candidates came from newly written tasks and unused reserves. Selection included human trials and removal of tasks judged to test the same rule; evaluation sets were balanced for human difficulty.
The paper describes human solvability checks and additional internal review. The change record later lists corrected cells and ambiguities in some public examples and test outputs.

The test uses two-dimensional grids. Its goals concern abstract reasoning and increasingly complex combinations of concepts. This packet contains no study establishing coverage of language, social interaction or real-world autonomous work.

A submitted grid matches only if its dimensions and cells match the reference. There is no credit for a partly correct grid, though a multi-input task can receive partial credit when some whole grids are correct.

The software averages within tasks and then across tasks. It does not report separate validated ability scores. The dataset’s all-inputs-correct description and software average are both supplied in Q5.

The public repository includes scorer tests for correct answers, wrong dimensions, changed pixels and missing outputs. The packet preparer inspected these cases but did not run a full scorer-validation study.
Human testing involved 407 people in 515 paid, 90-minute sessions on candidate tasks. The final dataset excludes some candidates.
The current verified-testing policy specifies one run rather than an average of runs. This packet includes no repeated-run variation estimates for a fixed AI system and setup.
Runner settings are configurable. The inspected sources provide no systematic study of instruction, representation or software changes.
The report gives model scores without corresponding repeat-run variance or confidence ranges. Human difficulty matching between sets is different.

The design explicitly targets resistance to exhaustive program search. The creators also compare tasks for redundancy. The packet contains no quantified demonstration that all alternative ways to earn credit have been eliminated.
Public tasks are accessible. For hidden remote tests, the policy specifies data-retention agreements and exposure monitoring, and acknowledges possible leakage.

The dataset instructions permit training on development tasks and warn against tuning using evaluation tasks. The verified-testing policy says testing is not a continuous optimization service for providers.
The creators connect performance to more general reasoning. This packet contains no study showing how ARC-AGI-2 scores predict success on other jobs. The reported experiments concern grid tasks.
Recorded human background factors showed no clear statistical relationship with performance. Verified tests record settings; other evaluation routes can differ.

Public data, running software and scorer tests are available. Hidden sets have controlled access. Policy states that public testing outputs, costs, durations and task scores are released; this packet did not audit the complete archive.
Public data carry an Apache 2.0 license. The policy sets restrictions for hidden data and describes confidentiality arrangements, provider handling and code review for selected submissions.

The dated change record identifies corrected tasks and links changes to commits. It does not provide a before-and-after score comparison for every affected model. ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 are separate versions.

Public descriptions use broad language about intelligence while describing a particular family of grid tasks. The information here includes those claims and the study limits; it does not include a universal intelligence score or real-world deployment study.

reading.title: What the AI is asked to do
reading.text: ARC-AGI-2 is a test developed by ARC Prize Foundation staff and partners to assess whether an AI can **work out a new rule from examples**. Each problem presents pairs of coloured grids, showing a starting grid alongside its correct finished grid. Using those examples, the AI must work out how to complete a new starting grid and return an answer with the right size and colour in every square. The creators designed these problems to require little specialist knowledge while encouraging the AI to combine ideas. Their aim is to study reasoning that goes beyond recalling facts or trying large numbers of possible programs, which they connect to progress toward more general, human-like AI.

reading.title: How the problems were chosen
reading.text: ARC-AGI-2’s developers began with a collection of newly written grid puzzles and puzzles prepared for earlier ARC work that had not been used. To help decide which puzzles to include and how difficult they were, the developers **conducted a study in which people tried solving them**. This involved **407 people taking part in 515 paid, 90-minute sessions**. The puzzles used in that study formed a larger pool than the final test, so the results do not all describe the final set. The developers also reviewed puzzles themselves and removed ones they judged could be solved by the same rule. The released benchmark contains **1,000 problems for practice and AI development**, along with **three test sets of 120 problems each**. These sets are called public, semi-private and private because access to their problems differs. Using the human participants’ results, the developers selected the three test sets to have similar difficulty for people. After release, they continued correcting the materials; a public change record lists fixes to some coloured squares and unclear examples.

reading.title: How answers earn points
reading.text: The AI is allowed **two attempts for each new input grid**, and it earns credit for that input only if an attempt matches the supplied answer in both size and every square’s colour. A nearly correct grid therefore receives no credit. A problem can contain several new inputs, however, so the official scoring software inspected for this survey calculates the fraction solved within each problem before averaging the problem scores. Solving one of two inputs, for example, earns **0.5 for that problem**. This differs from calling the whole problem “fully solved,” which the instructions published with the problems reserve for cases where every input is correct. The software does not provide separate scores established as measures of distinct skills. Its public tests cover correct answers, wrong sizes, changed squares and missing outputs; the survey preparer inspected those tests without independently testing the whole marking system.

reading.title: Testing conditions and changes in scores
reading.text: ARC Prize, the organization running the verified evaluations, specifies AI settings and a spending limit for the tests it verifies, although other testing routes may use different conditions. Its verified-testing policy uses **one run, rather than an average of repeated runs**. A technical report describing ARC-AGI-2’s development gives AI scores, but the materials reviewed here do not provide estimates or ranges showing how much the same AI’s score changes when the same test is repeated. Although the running software allows settings to be changed, those materials also contain no systematic study of the effects of changing instructions, grid presentation or software. Matching the test sets for human difficulty addresses a separate issue and does not measure these changes in AI scores.

reading.title: Prior exposure and ways to earn points
reading.text: The creators tried to limit ways of earning points without the intended reasoning by designing problems that resist searches through large numbers of possible programs and by checking for repeated solution rules. These steps do not establish that every such route to a high score has been ruled out. Prior exposure is another concern because anyone can see the public problems. For hidden tests sent to AI providers, ARC Prize describes agreements against retaining the data and monitoring of possible exposure, while acknowledging that information could still escape. To keep development separate from evaluation, **training on development problems is allowed, while changing a system specifically to improve on evaluation problems is discouraged**. ARC Prize also says its verified tests are not a service for repeatedly improving systems through its feedback.

reading.title: Comparisons, access and updates
reading.text: In the puzzle-solving study described above, the developers found no clear statistical relationship between performance and recorded background factors such as work and technical experience. For AI comparisons, verified tests record the settings used, though other testing routes may differ. Researchers can inspect **public problems, running software and marking tests**, while access to hidden problems is controlled. ARC Prize says it also releases public testing outputs, costs, times and problem scores, but the survey preparer did not check the complete archive. The public data use an Apache 2.0 licence; hidden-data rules address confidentiality, provider handling and code review for selected submissions. To help track revisions, a dated change record identifies corrected problems and exact code changes. It does not, however, recalculate every affected AI score, and ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 remain separate test versions.

reading.title: What the findings cover
reading.text: Although the creators connect ARC-AGI-2 to abstract reasoning and broader intelligence, the studies supplied here concern **two-dimensional grid problems**. This packet contains no study showing how scores predict success in language, social interaction or other real-world work, and it supplies no measure covering every kind of intelligence. These are **limits of the information available for this survey**: they leave those broader relationships unresolved, rather than showing that such relationships are impossible.

diagrams.title: Example: a problem with two new input grids

steps.title: Input 1: solved
steps.text: At least one permitted attempt matches the entire answer grid: 1.

steps.title: Input 2: unsolved
steps.text: Neither permitted attempt matches the entire answer grid: 0.

steps.title: Problem score: 0.5
steps.text: The inspected software calculates (1 + 0) ÷ 2. It then averages problem scores.

diagrams.caption: Illustration of the inspected software, not an observed AI result. A partly correct grid gets no credit. The dataset description calls the whole problem solved only when both inputs are correct.

benchmarks.name: Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)
benchmarks.subtitle: Advanced academic questions with definite answers
benchmarks.scope: The original 2,500-question HLE described in the supplied paper, with the simple public evaluation code inspected on 7 October 2026. This survey does not cover HLE-Rolling, HLE-Diamond or their evaluations with extra tools.
benchmarks.overview: Imagine a very difficult exam assembled by specialists from many subjects. The AI must select an answer or give a short answer; some questions also include an image. A separate AI marks the response against a supplied answer. HLE aims to measure advanced academic knowledge and reasoning. You do not need to know the subject answers to evaluate how this test is built, marked and interpreted.
benchmarks.intended_use: Using scores to compare AI systems on difficult academic questions, and considering claims about academic expertise beyond the exact questions.

facts.text: This section concerns original HLE: the 2,500-question public test described in the supplied paper. Public grading scripts are pinned for this packet. HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond are separate versions and are not the test being rated.

The authors aim to assess advanced academic knowledge and reasoning on questions with specific answers. They target language and image-capable AI systems, for capability measurement and research communication.

Questions span many academic subjects. About 24% are multiple-choice; the remainder require short answers. About 14% use images. A published biology example asks for a number about the anatomy of a hummingbird bone. No biology expertise is needed for this survey.

The supplied prediction script asks for an explanation, final answer and confidence percentage, and sends images when present. The README describes a default temperature of zero; in the inspected API call, the temperature-setting line is commented out. This packet concerns the simple evaluation, not tool-assisted HLE-Diamond.

An AI judge compares final answers with references, allowing equivalent forms. The script reports percentage correct, a confidence range, and how closely the AI’s stated confidence matches correctness.
The authors use expert-written, difficult questions with known answers to test academic knowledge and reasoning. They explicitly distinguish answering such questions from doing open-ended research.

Experts from many institutions supplied questions. Questions already answered by selected contemporary models were screened out before expert review. The resulting set was selected for difficulty, not randomly sampled from everyday academic work.

The paper describes expert review, organizer approval and audits. Appendix B.3 reports two 200-question audits and an estimated 15.4% expert-disagreement rate after the second. Disagreement is not the same as a confirmed wrong-answer rate.
The paper groups questions across numerous subjects and emphasizes mathematics. The accepted formats require definite answers. Open-ended research and creative work are outside the tested format.
The judge checks meaningful agreement with the reference, without re-solving the problem. This does not settle whether a disputed reference is correct.
Accuracy counts correct answers equally; subject mix therefore affects the overall score. Category results are reported, without a separate-ability validation study in the inspected material.
Judge software is public. Question audits are not automated-marking checks. No full judge-versus-expert agreement study was identified in the inspected sources.

The paper compares several named AI models and reports full-set and text-only results. Question contributors are experts, but this packet contains no matched human cohort taking the entire exam under the model-testing conditions.

The paper notes that a model can answer differently across attempts. The inspected sources do not provide a repeated-run stability study covering the main reported model comparisons. A generation-setting value alone is not a measurement of repeatability.

The paper supplies a standard response prompt and separates full-set from text-only results. This packet includes no systematic experiment measuring score changes after rewording prompts or changing grading-model versions.
The script’s approximate 95% range uses question count and fraction correct, not repeated AI runs or judge versions. Its separate calibration measure compares stated confidence with correctness.

Contributors were asked to avoid easy lookup and could modify questions when models guessed correctly with faulty reasoning. Multiple-choice options still allow guessing. No comprehensive study quantifying every possible shortcut is supplied here.

Authors retain a private set to assess overfitting. The public release includes a distinctive marker to help exclude it from future training, plus a warning against training on the test. Neither measure demonstrates what any particular model actually saw.

The repository warns against including benchmark data in training. The packet supplies no complete original-HLE rule set on repeated submissions, feedback access or separation of results from systems tuned on the test.

The paper says high scores concern closed-ended academic questions, not proof of autonomous research or general intelligence. This packet includes no measured relationship between HLE scores and success in independent scientific projects.

Image-capable and text-only systems do not necessarily receive the same question set. The paper labels text-only results. Questions are written in English and subject coverage is uneven. No comprehensive cross-language or cross-population comparison study is supplied here.

Public instructions and grading code are available. The dataset page requires accepting contact-sharing conditions before file access. The private set is not released. This packet was prepared without downloading gated questions or reproducing the model results.

The dataset page labels its license MIT and presents an access gate and a request not to redistribute test data. The code has an MIT license. The paper excludes certain dangerous-content categories during question collection. These are stated terms and precautions, not a legal assessment.

The site distinguishes original HLE, HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond. A separate rolling log records removals and re-additions. Those changes do not automatically describe original HLE, and this packet supplies no score-equivalence study across all versions.

The title suggests a final exam at the frontier of human knowledge. The paper narrows its interpretation to specific academic answers and explicitly says high performance alone would not establish autonomous research or general intelligence.

reading.title: What the AI is asked to do
reading.text: Humanity’s Last Exam, or HLE, aims to assess advanced academic knowledge and reasoning in AI systems that handle text or text and images. This survey focuses on **the original HLE, which contains 2,500 difficult questions**, rather than the separate HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond versions. About **24% of its questions are multiple-choice**, while the rest require short answers, and about **14% include an image**. A published biology example asks for a number about the anatomy of a hummingbird bone. You do not need to solve that problem to complete this survey; it illustrates the kind of specialist question the AI receives. Across these formats, HLE asks for specific answers rather than the completion of an open-ended research project.

reading.title: How the questions were chosen and checked
reading.text: Experts from many institutions contributed questions covering a range of subjects, with particular emphasis on mathematics. Before expert review, questions that selected AI models could already answer were screened out, so the resulting set was **deliberately chosen to be difficult**, rather than randomly drawn from everyday academic work. HLE’s creators describe their development process in a research paper, which reports expert review and organizer approval, followed by two further checks of 200 questions each. After the second check, the authors estimated an **expert-disagreement rate of 15.4%**. That figure concerns disagreements about questions or answers; it should not be read as the percentage confirmed to be wrong. Because the test requires specific answers, it also leaves creative work and open-ended research outside its answer format.

reading.title: Instructions and marking
reading.text: HLE’s public evaluation software gives the AI each question, includes an image when needed, and asks it to return an explanation, a final answer and a percentage stating its confidence. The instructions for that software describe a default “temperature” of zero, a setting intended to reduce randomness, but the line that sends this setting is **disabled in the inspected code**. Once a response is produced, a separate **AI judge compares the final answer with the supplied reference answer**, accepting different wording when the meaning is the same. Because the judge is instructed to compare answers rather than solve the problem independently, agreement does not establish that the reference itself is correct. The judging code is public, but the inspected sources contain no full study comparing its marks with expert marks. The expert reviews of the questions described earlier therefore do not, by themselves, establish that the automatic marking is accurate.

reading.title: What the reported numbers mean
reading.text: HLE reports **accuracy as the percentage of answers marked correct**, with each question counting equally. As a result, the mix of subjects affects the total score. The paper also reports results by subject, although the inspected material does not establish that these are separate measures of distinct skills. Alongside accuracy, the public scoring software calculates an **approximate 95% confidence range** using the number of questions and the fraction marked correct. This range describes score uncertainty under the calculation’s assumptions; it does not measure the effects of repeating the AI run or changing the judge. A separate calculation compares the AI’s stated confidence with how often its answers are correct, so **confidence in an answer and uncertainty in a test score refer to different things**.

reading.title: Comparisons and repeated testing
reading.text: To put results in context, the paper compares named AI models and reports scores for both the full question set and text-only questions. Although experts helped create the questions, this packet contains **no matched group of people taking the whole exam under the AI testing conditions**. The paper also notes that an AI can answer differently on different attempts, but the inspected sources do not provide a repeated-run study covering the main comparisons. Nor do they provide a systematic study of reworded instructions or changes to the judging AI. Using a fixed setting or a standard instruction therefore does not, on its own, establish how stable the reported scores are.

reading.title: Prior exposure and ways to earn points
reading.text: To reduce easy ways of gaining points, contributors were asked to avoid questions answerable by a simple lookup and could revise questions when an AI guessed correctly through faulty reasoning. Multiple-choice questions still allow guessing, however, and the supplied material does not measure every possible way of earning points without the intended knowledge or reasoning. The authors also retain a **private test set** to help assess whether improvements are specific to the public questions. For the public data, a distinctive text marker helps people identify material to exclude from future AI training, while the instructions warn against training on the test. These precautions do not establish what a particular AI has already seen. The packet also lacks a complete original-HLE policy covering repeated submissions, access to feedback and the reporting of systems trained specifically on the test.

reading.title: Access, fair comparisons and updates
reading.text: Fair comparisons depend partly on which questions each system receives. Systems that use images and those that only use text do not necessarily answer the same set, so the paper labels text-only results. The questions are in English and subjects are not equally represented; the supplied material contains no comprehensive study of comparisons across languages or populations. Public instructions and marking code allow some inspection, but downloading the dataset requires accepting contact-sharing conditions, and the private set is not released. The dataset page lists an MIT licence and asks users not to redistribute test data, while the code also has an MIT licence. The authors describe excluding certain kinds of dangerous content during collection. The survey preparer inspected the available documentation without downloading the gated questions or rerunning the AI evaluations. When comparing results over time, the edition also matters: HLE-Rolling has its own record of removed and restored questions, and **those changes do not automatically describe original HLE**. No study establishing equivalent scores across original HLE, HLE-Rolling and HLE-Diamond is supplied here.

reading.title: What the findings cover
reading.text: HLE’s title suggests a final exam at the edge of human knowledge, but the paper limits its interpretation to difficult academic questions with definite answers. It explicitly states that **a high score alone does not establish general intelligence or the ability to conduct independent research**. Consistent with that limit, this packet contains no measured relationship between HLE scores and success on independent scientific projects. Such gaps leave broader claims unresolved; they do not, by themselves, show that the benchmark fails.

diagrams.title: How an HLE answer is marked

steps.title: Receive a question
steps.text: Text, sometimes with an image; choose an option or give a short answer.

steps.title: Give a response
steps.text: The AI provides an explanation, a final answer and its stated confidence.

steps.title: Compare with the reference
steps.text: A separate AI judge checks the final answer against the supplied answer. Equivalent meanings can count.

diagrams.caption: Process diagram based on the simple evaluation code. The judge is not asked to solve the question independently.

diagrams.title: Three different numbers in the results

steps.title: Accuracy
steps.text: What percentage of answers were marked correct?

steps.title: Score range
steps.text: How uncertain is that percentage under the calculation used? This is not a repeated-run test.

steps.title: Confidence check
steps.text: Does how confident the AI says it is match how often it is correct?

diagrams.caption: These are separate summaries of the answers. None substitutes for measuring changes across repeated runs.

sources.note: Primary source, inspected at the pinned commit. Used for setup, averaging, dataset paths and the submission procedure. The README gives an approximate rulebook length that differs from the paper; the example uses the paper’s 140-page description.

sources.title: DesignQA: Evaluation driver
sources.note: Primary code inspection. Checked optional subset arguments, the six-score average and results-file output. No end-to-end model evaluation was run.

sources.title: DesignQA: Metric implementations
sources.note: Primary code inspection. Checked answer normalization, comma-separated rule parsing, component synonyms, yes/no extraction and explanation metrics. Inspection is not a complete scorer validation.

sources.note: Recursive GitHub tree inspected at the commit; tags and releases endpoints returned empty lists on 2026-10-06. No license or changelog file was found in this inventory. This is a bounded file/document check, not a legal conclusion or proof that no policies exist elsewhere.

sources.title: DesignQA: Released LLaVA retrieval predictions
sources.note: CSV inspected: 1,190 rows, with question, ground_truth and model_prediction columns. Establishes that some predictions are available. Its row count differs from the paper’s 1,192 retrieval questions, so it is not assumed to be a complete, exact paper-run archive.

sources.note: Seven rows inspected, including prediction, answer and category columns. The metrics file also contains commented test calls. Test data exist; no executed assertion suite or published scorer error rate was established.

terms: Benchmark
A test used to assess an AI system.
Benchmark version
A particular edition or revision of a test. Its problems, answers or marking rules may differ from an earlier edition. The edition matters when comparing scores.
Ability or skill
Something the AI is meant to be able to do, such as finding a rule in a pattern or answering a science question. A score on one skill does not automatically describe every skill.
AI system or model
The software taking the test, sometimes with extra tools.
Task, item or test problem
One question or puzzle the AI must solve.
Prompt
The instructions and information given to the AI.
Reference answer
The supplied answer used to mark the AI’s response.
Score
The result of marking, such as percentage correct.
Evaluation set
The group of problems used to test a system. A separate development set may be used to improve it.
Scoring software or harness
Code that calculates scores or runs the test.
Score uncertainty
How uncertain a score estimate is under the method used to calculate it. This is different from the AI saying it is confident.
Intended use
The claim or decision a score is meant to support.
example_intro: DesignQA tests AI on questions about vehicle drawings and engineering rules. Each “Example” shows a brief answer from the existing DesignQA review and why that answer was chosen. These are worked examples, not an answer key for ARC-AGI-2 or HLE. Your own choices remain blank.
example_scope: The DesignQA examples summarize a review of the 2024 paper and public scoring software, checked on 6 October 2026. They illustrate reviewer judgments and are not an answer key for the other benchmarks.
